newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S. cement dumping ruling imminent - Mexico firms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cement dumping ruling imminent - Mexico firms.

text.p: Mexican cement companies were expecting a final decision later Wednesday from the U.S. Commerce Department on charges that Mexico "dumped" cement on the U.S. market from August 1994 to July 1995, industry sources said.
Last September the U.S. government decided in a preliminary review to increase compulsory taxes on Mexican cement imports to 107.8 percent from 42 percent as part of a larger dumping investigation.
The long-standing trade dispute began when U.S companies in 1988 accused Mexican cement firms of exporting the product at prices below those in its domestic market.
"The law requires that the ruling be made today and, generally, they do it in the afternoon," Grupo Cementos Chihuahua (GCC) investor relations director Jaime Fernandez said.
GCC and Cemex are the Mexican cement companies most targeted in the U.S. dumping case. A Cemex source close to the process said the company is expecting a decision "within the week."

Mexican cement companies currently pay a tax of 62 percent per tonne exported, as part of a September 1996 U.S. Commerce decision. Any tax rise from the review would take effect in the middle of April and not be retroactive, Fernandez added.
"What they (the U.S. Commerce Department) could do is confirm the tax, but not reduce or eliminate it," Mexico City ABN Amro Bank analyst Carlos Perezalonso said.
While Cemex officials declined to comment on a possible decision, GCC said the revision could boost the tax to 90 percent per tonne for cement exports.
"Last year we expected good news," UBS Securities analyst in New York Alvaro Shiraishi said. "But considering how things are shaping up, they are going to raise (the tariffs) again."

He added that the decision should affect GCC more than Cemex, because the smaller GCC has no alternative in exporting to the U.S. market. In contrast, Cemex can export to the United States from its operations in Spain and Venezuela, Shiraishi said.
